blocks.prompt: Read this out loud
blocks.text: This is a seal. The seal lives in the cold sea. It has thick fur and big round eyes. Look at its whiskers. The whiskers can feel the water move. A fish swims by. The water wiggles. The seal feels the wiggle. Now the seal knows where the fish went. Down it goes. The seal swims fast. On land it has no feet for walking. It wiggles on its belly.

blocks.prompt: The Seal Takes a Deep Breath
blocks.text: A seal is a mammal, like you. It breathes air. But a seal can stay under the water for a long, long time. Watch it before it dives. The seal breathes out. That looks wrong. You would fill your lungs up. The seal empties them instead. It keeps the air it needs in its blood, not in its chest. Then its heart slows down. Thump. Thump. Very slow. A harbor seal can stay under for almost half an hour. Under its skin is a thick layer of fat called blubber. The blubber keeps the seal warm in the cold sea. On land a seal cannot walk. Its back feet are flippers, and they point backward. So it humps along on its belly. It looks silly. It does not care.

blocks.prompt: The Whiskers That Follow a Ghost
blocks.text: The sea is dark. Down deep, a seal can barely see its own flippers. So how does it ever find dinner? The answer is on its face. A seal's whiskers are not like a cat's. They are thick, and they are wavy, like a tiny row of ripples. When a fish swims past, it leaves a trail behind it in the water. The trail is a line of small swirls, and it hangs there for about half a minute after the fish has gone. You could never see that trail. A seal can feel it. Scientists tested this. They covered a harbor seal's eyes so it could not see, and put headphones over its ears so it could not hear. Then they sent a small machine swimming across the pool. The seal came along after it, whiskers out, and followed the trail the machine had left, turn for turn, all the way to the end. Think about what that means. A seal can track a fish it has never seen and never heard. It hunts a ghost, and it catches it.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: A seal breathes out before it dives
Myoglobin makes seal muscle almost black
The diving reflex slows the heart right down
Its spleen stores blood like a spare tank
Harbor seal: about 30 minutes on one breath
Elephant seal: 2 hours, and nearly a mile and a half down

blocks.prompt: One Breath, Two Hours
blocks.text: Every seal that dives is running a countdown. It is a mammal. It breathes air, exactly as you do, and down where it is going there is none. Watch what a seal does just before it drops. It breathes out. That seems backward. A person about to dive fills their lungs as full as they will go. The seal empties them on purpose. Air squeezed under the pressure of deep water pushes nitrogen into the blood, and nitrogen in the blood is dangerous. Human divers get sick that way. So the seal takes its oxygen down somewhere safer: in its blood and in its muscles. A seal carries about twice as much blood for its size as a human does. Its muscles are loaded with a protein called myoglobin, which grabs oxygen and holds on to it. There is so much myoglobin in there that seal muscle is not pink. It is almost black. Then the diving reflex takes over. The seal's heart slows down until it is beating only a handful of times a minute. Blood vessels near the skin clamp shut, and the blood that is left goes to the two organs that cannot wait: the heart and the brain. The flippers and the gut are told to make do. There is one more reserve. A seal's spleen is enormous, and it holds a private store of blood already loaded with oxygen. As the dive begins, the spleen squeezes, and that hidden supply joins the rest. The seal has packed a spare tank inside itself. A harbor seal can stay under for about half an hour on that one breath out. An elephant seal can manage two hours, and take it nearly a mile and a half straight down.

answers: pressure would push nitrogen from lung air into its blood, which is dangerous; it stores oxygen in blood and muscle instead
it is packed with myoglobin, the protein that holds oxygen
(inference: the heart and brain cannot wait, so vessels near the skin shut and blood is saved for them)
(it holds a hidden supply of oxygen-rich blood and releases it when the dive starts)

notes: Weddell seal: the farthest south of any mammal
It lives under solid ice all winter
It saws its breathing hole open with its teeth

It dives about 2,000 feet, for over an hour

blocks.prompt: The Seal at the Bottom of the World
blocks.text: No mammal lives farther south than the Weddell seal. It spends its winters underneath the solid ice of Antarctica, in water sitting at about 28 degrees Fahrenheit, colder than the freezing point of fresh water and held liquid only by its salt. Above the seal is a ceiling of ice several feet thick. Above that is the dark, and the wind, and nothing. This is a strange address to choose. But look at what is not there. Under the ice there are no orcas, and no leopard seals hunting, because they cannot get in either. The Weddell seal has traded away the open sea for a room that nothing else can enter. The rent is a hole. A seal must breathe. So it makes its own hole in the ceiling, and then it has to keep it, and it keeps it with its teeth. The seal swims up, opens its mouth, and rasps its canines and its front teeth across the underside of the ice, back and forth, sawing, widening the opening before the cold can seal it shut. It does this all winter. It does it for years. Teeth do not grow back. Every hour of rasping wears them down a little more, and an old Weddell seal's teeth are stumps, cracked and worn to the gum. When the teeth fail, the seal can no longer keep its hole open. When the hole closes, the seal drowns beneath a roof it can no longer cut. Biologists who study these animals say the same thing again and again: a Weddell seal does not really die of old age. It dies of its own teeth. In between, though, it is magnificent. It dives two thousand feet down into black water and stays for more than an hour on a single breath, hunting fish it finds by feel. It sings underwater in long falling whistles that sound like something recorded on another planet, and the sound carries for miles beneath the ice. That is the deal the Weddell seal made. A safe room, a good life, and a bill that comes due in enamel.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Seals are carnivorans: kin to bears, dogs, and weasels
Puijila, found 2007 on Devon Island, had four webbed feet
A front flipper still holds five fingers inside it
Undulated whiskers stay quiet enough to feel a wake
Elephant seals sleep about 2 hours a day, while sinking
Every pinniped must still be born in the air

blocks.prompt: The Bargain the Seal Made
blocks.text: A seal is a land animal that changed its mind. Look at the skeleton and it gives itself away. Inside each front flipper is a hand: an upper arm bone, two forearm bones, a wrist, and five fingers, shortened and bound together under the skin, but all of them there, in the same order as yours. Seals did not rise out of the ocean. They walked into it. Their ancestors were carnivorans, sitting on the same branch of the mammal family tree that produced bears, dogs, and weasels, and more than twenty million years ago some of them began spending more time in the water than out of it. In 2007, on Devon Island in the Canadian Arctic, researchers dug up one of those in-between animals. They named it Puijila. It was roughly the size of a river otter, and it had four legs, four webbed feet, a long tail, and no flippers at all. It swam by paddling. It is a photograph of the decision being made. Here is the thing worth noticing. Every advantage a seal has today was bought by giving something up. That is the honest shape of the story. It gave up walking. A true seal's hind flippers point permanently backward and cannot swing forward beneath the body, which is why a seal on a beach hauls itself along in a heaving belly crawl, and why a sea lion, which kept that joint, can trot. Put the same animal in water and those flippers sweep side to side and it becomes something else entirely: fast, silent, exact. It gave up seeing. Not completely, but the deep sea is dark and murky, and eyes are only so useful there. So the seal moved its hunting into its face. Its whiskers are thick and wavy, and the wave is the whole point: the ripples cancel the noise a straight whisker would make as water rushed past it, leaving the whisker quiet enough to feel something almost impossibly faint. A swimming fish drags a wake behind it, a hanging line of swirls that lingers for perhaps half a minute. In one famous experiment, a blindfolded harbor seal wearing headphones tracked the wake of a small submarine across a pool, following every turn it had made, long after it had gone. The seal was hunting a fish that was not there anymore, and the whiskers did not care. It gave up breathing, in a way. A diving seal exhales first, because lungs full of air become a liability under pressure, and it carries its oxygen in its blood and in its muscle instead. Its muscle holds so much myoglobin that it is nearly black. Its spleen waits like a spare tank, loaded with oxygen-rich blood, and squeezes it into circulation as the dive begins. Its heart drops to a handful of beats a minute. Its blood abandons the skin and the gut and serves only the brain and the heart. An elephant seal can hold that arrangement together for two hours and carry it nearly a mile and a half down. It even gave up sleep, or rebuilt it. In 2023, scientists fitted northern elephant seals with brain-wave sensors and found that out at sea they sleep about two hours a day, in naps of ten minutes or so, taken while falling. The seal stops swimming partway down a dive, goes limp, and spirals slowly toward the bottom, asleep, far out of reach of the sharks and orcas waiting at the surface. Then it wakes, and swims back up to breathe. There is one thing it could not give up. A seal must still be born on solid ground, on a beach or on the ice, dry, into the open air. Every year the whole species has to return and be a land animal again for a while, and it is always here, hauled out and clumsy and slow, that people have found it easiest to kill. That is the bargain. Nothing the seal gained was free.
